lessons.title: Articles der, die, das
lessons.summary: Every German noun has a gender, shown by its article. Learn each noun with its article and half the grammar comes for free.

cards.title: When do you need them?
cards.body: Whenever you name a thing: in a shop, at home, at work. **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine), **das** (neuter). The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: **das** Mädchen (the girl) is neuter!

cards.title: the or a?
cards.body: **der/die/das** = the: something known. **ein/eine** = a: something new in the conversation. Masculine and neuter share **ein**, feminine takes **eine**.

examples.german: Das ist **ein** Kuli. **Der** Kuli ist blau.
examples.english: This is a pen. The pen is blue.

cards.title: Endings that help
cards.body: You can often guess: **-ung, -heit, -keit, -ion, -schaft, -e** → mostly **die**. **-chen, -lein, -ment, -um** → **das**. **-er** (people), **-ismus**, days, months and seasons → **der**.
cards.tip: Colour-code your flashcards: blue der, red die, green das.

cards.title: Asking what something is
cards.body: **Was ist das?** – **Das ist ein/eine …**. Here **das** means 'this/that' and never changes, whatever the gender of the noun.

examples.german: Was ist das? – Das ist **eine** Uhr.
examples.english: What is that? – That is a clock.

examples.german: Wie heißt das auf Deutsch? – **Der** Schlüssel.
examples.english: What's that called in German? – The key.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't guess from the meaning: **das** Mädchen, **der** Löffel, **die** Gabel, **das** Messer. Always learn the noun **with** its article, never alone.

games.prompt: der, die or das? (look at the ending)
games.explanation: -ung, -ion → die; -chen, -um → das; people in -er and days → der.
der and das → ein, die → eine.

games.prompt: Was ist das? – Das ist ___ Lampe.
games.english: What is that? – That is a lamp.
games.explanation: die Lampe is feminine, so 'a' is eine.

lessons.title: Plural of nouns
lessons.summary: In the plural every article becomes die, but the noun can end in five different ways. A few patterns make it much easier.

cards.title: When do you need it?
cards.body: Shopping lists, counting things, talking about your family: **zwei Kinder**, **drei Äpfel**. Good news: in the plural the article is always **die** — no more der/die/das.

examples.english: the tables, the lamps, the books

cards.title: The five patterns
cards.body: German adds **-e, -(e)n, -er, -s** or nothing, sometimes with an umlaut (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü).

rows: der Tisch → die Tisch**e**, der Stuhl → die St**ü**hl**e**
die Lampe → die Lampe**n**, die Frau → die Frau**en**
der Lehrer → die Lehrer, die Mutter → die M**ü**tter

cards.title: Good guesses
cards.body: Feminine nouns, especially in **-e, -ung, -ion**, mostly take **-(e)n**. Words from English or ending in a vowel like -a, -o, -i take **-s**. Masculine and neuter nouns in **-er, -el, -chen** often add nothing.
cards.tip: Always learn the plural with the noun: der Tisch, -e.

cards.title: kein in the plural
cards.body: There's no plural of **ein**: you just say the noun. The negative is **keine**.

examples.english: I have photos. – I have no photos.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't put **-s** everywhere like in English: die Tisch**e**, not 'Tischs'. And don't forget the umlaut: die B**ü**cher, die M**ä**nner.

games.explanation: Feminine nouns take -(e)n; words ending in a vowel like -o or -y take -s.
-er always brings an umlaut when possible; nouns in -er often add nothing.
der Apfel → die Äpfel: no ending, just an umlaut.

lessons.title: Compound nouns
lessons.summary: German glues nouns together to make new ones. Once you see the parts, long words become easy.

cards.title: Why German loves them
cards.body: Instead of 'the door of the kitchen', German says **die Küchentür**. You meet compounds everywhere: in the flat, in the shop, on signs. Split them into parts and you can often guess the meaning.

cards.title: The last word is the boss
cards.body: The **last** part says what the thing is and gives the **article** and the **plural**. The parts before only describe it.
cards.tip: Haustür is a door, Türschild is a sign: read from the end.

cards.title: Little linking letters
cards.body: Sometimes a letter joins the parts: **-s-** (die Arbeit**s**zeit), **-n-** or **-en-** (die Tasche**n**lampe). The first part can also be a verb stem or an adjective: **Schreib**tisch, **Groß**stadt.

cards.title: Writing and stress
cards.body: A compound is **one word**, written together with one capital letter. The stress is usually on the **first** part: **KÜ**chentür.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't take the article of the first word: it's **die** Haustür, not 'das Haustür'. And don't split it in two words like in English.

games.explanation: The first part describes, the last part names the thing.

games.prompt: Which article? (look at the last part)
games.explanation: die Tür, das Zimmer, der Schlüssel, die Lampe, der Schrank.

lessons.title: nicht or kein?
lessons.summary: German has two ways to say no: kein for nouns, nicht for everything else. Plus doch, the magic yes.

cards.title: When do you need it?
cards.body: Whenever you disagree or correct someone: **Das ist kein Kuli, das ist ein Bleistift.** Or when you say what you don't do: **Ich wohne nicht in Berlin.**

examples.german: Ist das ein Handy? – Nein, das ist **kein** Handy.
examples.english: Is that a phone? – No, that isn't a phone.

cards.title: kein = not a / no
cards.body: Use **kein** for nouns with **ein** or with no article. It takes the same endings as ein: **kein** (der/das), **keine** (die and plural).

cards.title: nicht for the rest
cards.body: Use **nicht** with verbs, adjectives, names and nouns with **der/die/das** or my/your. **nicht** goes at the end of the sentence or before the word it negates.

examples.german: Das ist **nicht** der Bus nach Bonn.
examples.english: That isn't the bus to Bonn.

cards.tip: Can you say 'a' or nothing in front of the noun? → kein. Otherwise → nicht.

cards.title: Ja, nein, doch
cards.body: To contradict a **negative** question, don't say ja: say **doch**.

examples.english: Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!

examples.german: Hast du keine Zeit? – **Doch**, ein bisschen.
examples.english: Don't you have time? – Yes I do, a little.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Not 'nicht ein': say **kein**. Not 'Ich habe nicht Zeit': say **Ich habe keine Zeit**. And answer a negative question with **doch**, not ja.

games.explanation: kein/keine replace ein or no article; nicht negates verbs and adjectives.

games.prompt: Bist du nicht müde? – ___, ich bin sehr müde!
games.english: Aren't you tired? – Yes I am, I'm very tired!

games.explanation: kein follows ein; the plural takes keine.
